If you are in Luzon this weekend, skip the gauges. Open [PAGASA](https://bagong.pagasa.dost.gov.ph/). They have named **Tropical Depression Pilandok**, a leftover look at **Saudel**, and a **southwest monsoon** already dumping hard rain on western Luzon. As of Sunday morning they had **red flood warnings** on parts of Bataan, Zambales, Tarlac, Pampanga, and Bulacan. Metro Manila was under yellow in several cities.

That is the useful information. This site does not outrank it.

## What you should actually do

**If PAGASA or your barangay says move, move.** Take papers, medicine, and phones in a dry bag. Do not wait for a chart from us.

**If you are in a red or orange rainfall warning:** stay off swollen rivers and low roads. Do not drive through water you cannot see the bottom of. Charge power banks while the line still works.

**If you are not under a warning:** you do not need to leave town because a website exists. Keep drinking water and a week of medicine the way people already do in habagat season. Check on one neighbor who cannot move fast.

**Do not** sell land, change countries, or stop a prescribed treatment because of anything on this page.

## What our board is for — and what it is not

PAGASA tells you about **the next 24–72 hours** in the Philippines.

Our board is trying to answer a slower question: when a month or a season looks odd, odd compared with **what**? We keep a 30-year rain and temperature memory at nine places, including **Ubay**, plus a daily fire-hotspot count and a Pacific ocean index.

It is a memory aid. It is not a warning office. It cannot see your street. It cannot see most of Mindanao or the Visayas as a live flood map. When a box on our fire map comes back empty, that box is **blind**, not safe.

## What the slower instruments said this week

**Pacific ocean index (ONI), May–July 2026: +1.39.**  
That number comes from [NOAA CPC](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/data/indices/oni.ascii.txt). In plain speech: the central Pacific surface has been warmer than its own recent average. That is **not** why Bataan is flooding today. Today’s water is monsoon plus a depression, which PAGASA already named. A warm Pacific can tilt *later* seasons in some places and not others. We will not pretend we know your barangay’s next six months from one index.

**Rain file we use for history: last month on the server is July.**  
August from that global product is late. Late is not drought. Do not read a missing file as “the rains failed.”

**Fire satellites, one daily pass: about 5,000 hotspots.**  
One large western-southern box returned zero while another box returned thousands. Treat zero as “we did not see,” not “nothing is burning.” If you live with grass or forest fire risk, use your national fire map, not our four boxes.

**Atlantic current (AMOC):** not updated here. Anyone using rain in Ubay to “prove” that current has shifted is making a category error.

## If you do not live in the Philippines

Same rule: **your** met service first.  
[BMKG](https://www.bmkg.go.id/) for Indonesia. [INMET](https://portal.inmet.gov.br/) for Brazil. [NiMet](https://nimet.gov.ng/) for Nigeria. [KMD](https://meteo.go.ke/) for Kenya. [SMN](https://smn.conagua.gob.mx/) for Mexico. [NOAA](https://www.weather.gov/) for the United States.

A warm Pacific index is a background fact. It does not tell a farmer in Nairobi and a clerk in Paris the same story. A small test we ran on 29 winters even pointed **opposite ways** at Ubay and Nairobi. So we will not issue one global instruction.

## What this page refuses to do

It will not tell you the world is ending this week.  
It will not tell you to move to a “Goldilocks band.”  
It will not treat nine dots as a habitable-site survey.  
It will not quietly upgrade a parked claim because the Pacific number is large.

If a later brief has to walk something back, it will say so in the first paragraph.
